pages.title: Foundations: Hope is Not a Strategy
bulletPoints: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) treats operations as an engineering problem solved with software.
Traditional conflict: Product developers want rapid velocity; operations teams want absolute stability.
SRE bridges the gap: Software engineers tasked with designing, operating, and scaling large production systems.
Key rule: At least 50% of an SRE engineer’s time must be dedicated to pure engineering (software projects, automation).

pages.title: SRE vs DevOps: Shared Cultural Principles
bulletPoints: DevOps defines high-level philosophy; SRE provides concrete operational implementations.
Reduce organizational silos: SREs embed with development teams and share ownership of production releases.
Accept failure as normal: Hardware will fail, networks will partition, bugs will slip into production.
Implement gradual change: Small canary rollouts minimize blast radius when unexpected regressions occur.

pages.title: Service Level Terminology: SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs
bulletPoints: Service Level Indicator (SLI): A quantifiable metric measuring service behavior (e.g. latency, error rate).
Service Level Objective (SLO): A target percentage or range agreed internally that the service must achieve.
Service Level Agreement (SLA): A formal external business contract with customers incurring legal/financial penalties.
SRE principle: SLOs must always be stricter than SLAs to catch and resolve regressions before penalties trigger.
pages.formulaOrSummary: SLI: Metric -> SLO: Target -> SLA: Contract

pages.title: Defining Meaningful SLIs in Production
bulletPoints: User-centric measurement: Measure SLIs from the customer’s perspective, not merely server CPU saturation.
Request-driven services: Request latency, HTTP status code distribution (2xx/3xx vs 5xx), and throughput.
Data pipeline services: Processing lag, pipeline throughput (records/sec), and end-to-end data freshness.
Storage systems: Availability of read/write operations, data durability, and tail read latency.

pages.title: Choosing Realistic SLOs & Target Windows
bulletPoints: Never promise 100% reliability: 100% is the wrong target for virtually everything because users cannot tell the difference.
The edge problem: User phone networks, ISP hiccups, and Wi-Fi drops limit user-perceived uptime to 99.9% or 99.99%.
Rolling measurement windows: A 30-day rolling window gives a smooth, consistent view without arbitrary calendar resets.
Cost escalation: Moving from 99.9% (43 mins downtime/month) to 99.99% (4 mins) costs 10x more engineering effort.

pages.title: The Error Budget: Balancing Velocity and Stability
bulletPoints: The Error Budget is the exact mathematical inverse of the SLO (e.g., a 99.9% SLO leaves a 0.1% Error Budget).
Error budget as shared currency: The product team can burn this budget on risky new feature releases and experiments.
Budget exhausted consequence: Feature releases freeze immediately, and all engineering shifts to reliability work.
Outcome: Development and operations teams are naturally aligned rather than fighting over releases.

pages.title: Calculating and Spending Error Budgets Safely
bulletPoints: Burn rate calculation: Burn rate indicates how rapidly a service is exhausting its error budget relative to the window.
Burn rate = 1: The service will consume 100% of its budget over the entire 30-day window.
Burn rate = 14.4: The service will burn through 2% of its monthly budget in just one hour.
Multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting: Alert pagers on high burn rates (e.g. 14.4x), while ticket low burn rates.
pages.formulaOrSummary: Burn Rate = (Error Rate / Allowed Error Rate)

pages.title: Eliminating Toil: Defining Toil vs Engineering Work
bulletPoints: Toil is operational work tied to running a service that is repetitive, manual, tactical, and lacks enduring value.
Toil scales linearly with service size: If doubling traffic doubles operational tasks, the team is drowning in toil.
Engineering work creates enduring value: Writing autonomous remediation daemons, self-healing controllers, and tools.
The 50% rule: SRE teams track and cap toil strictly at 50%; excess operational load is routed back to product teams.

pages.title: Engineering Strategies for Automating Operational Work
bulletPoints: Automate incrementally: Start by documenting standard operating procedures (runbooks), then script them.
Self-healing systems: Systems should detect failing pods, corrupt disks, or network blackholes and remediate autonomously.
Idempotent operations: Scripts and automations must be safe to execute multiple times without unexpected side-effects.
Human-in-the-loop fallback: Provide clean override levers so on-call engineers can halt runaway automation if needed.

pages.title: The Four Golden Signals of Distributed Systems
bulletPoints: Latency: The time it takes to service a request (differentiate between successful request latency vs failed error latency).
Traffic: A measure of how much demand is placed on your system (e.g., HTTP requests/sec or concurrent streaming sessions).
Errors: The rate of requests that fail, either explicitly (HTTP 500) or implicitly (wrong payload or empty results).
Saturation: How "full" the service is, measuring constrained resources (CPU, RAM memory, IOPS, disk, or connection pools).
pages.formulaOrSummary: Golden Signals: Latency · Traffic · Errors · Saturation

pages.title: White-Box vs Black-Box Monitoring & Probing
bulletPoints: White-box monitoring: Introspecting internal system state using logs, traces, and metrics (Prometheus, OpenTelemetry).
Black-box monitoring: Testing externally visible system behavior from external probes (probing synthetic user journeys).
Complementary power: Black-box testing tells you the site is down; white-box metrics tell you which component broke and why.
Synthetic probers: Run scheduled fake user transactions (e.g. login, add-to-cart) to detect broken paths before users do.

pages.title: Effective Alerting: Reducing Pager Fatigue
bulletPoints: Every alert that pages an engineer must be urgent, actionable, and require human intuition immediately.
Non-actionable noise: If an alert fires and the engineer simply acknowledges and sleeps, delete that alert immediately.
Symptom-based alerting: Alert on broken user journeys (elevated 5xx rate), not cause-based noise (single server CPU at 95%).
Link directly to runbooks: Every alert notification should include a clickable link to a step-by-step triage guide.

pages.title: Incident Management: Roles & Clear Communication
bulletPoints: Incident Commander (IC): Leads the response, coordinates delegates, and makes high-level decisions; does not debug.
Operations Lead (Ops): The hands on keyboard executing diagnostics, rollbacks, and mitigations.
Communications Lead (Comms): Updates status dashboards, executive stakeholders, and customer support channels.
Structured response: Clear role segregation prevents chaos and duplicate efforts during high-pressure outages.
pages.formulaOrSummary: Incident Command: Commander · Ops Lead · Comms Lead

pages.title: Blameless Postmortems: Culture of Learning
bulletPoints: Core tenet: Assume that everyone involved had good intentions and acted on the best information available at the time.
Blame stifles truth: Punishing mistakes leads engineers to hide failures and prevents discovering systemic weaknesses.
Focus on system design: Why did the system allow a human to accidentally drop a production database?
Key artifacts: Detailed timeline of events, root cause analysis, what went well, what went poorly, and action items.

pages.title: Tracking Action Items & Preventing Recurrence
bulletPoints: Action items from postmortems must be tracked as high-priority engineering tasks with assigned owners and due dates.
Defense in depth: Add automated regression tests, guardrails, policy-as-code validators, and architectural buffers.
Chaos validation: After fixing an issue, intentionally inject the same failure in staging to prove the remediation works.
Review cadence: Regularly review open postmortem action items to ensure reliability fixes do not get neglected.

pages.title: Graceful Degradation & Emergency Response
bulletPoints: Degrade non-essential functionality: During peak loads, turn off expensive recommendations and personalizations.
Static fallback pages: Serve cached static snapshots from CDN edges when backend databases are struggling.
Prioritize critical paths: In an e-commerce platform, checkout and payment must survive even if search is impaired.
Feature flags: Equip all high-overhead features with kill-switches to shed compute cycles during emergencies.

pages.title: Managing Overload: Rate Limiting & Circuit Breaking
bulletPoints: Rate limiting: Protect upstream services from sudden traffic spikes using token bucket or leaky bucket algorithms.
Circuit breaking: Automatically stop routing requests to an unhealthy dependency to allow it time to recover.
States of a circuit breaker: Closed (healthy, requests flow), Open (failing, fast-fail), Half-Open (trial requests).
Preventing thundering herds: Cache responses locally and synchronize cache re-population across instances.

pages.title: Cascading Failures: Deadlines, Backoff & Jitter
bulletPoints: Cascading failure: A failure in one component causes failures in dependent components, crashing the entire cluster.
Deadlines / Timeouts: Propagate request deadlines across all RPC hops so dead requests are stopped early.
Exponential backoff: Increase retry delays exponentially (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s) to avoid overwhelming a struggling server.
Random jitter: Add randomized delay to retries to desynchronize retry spikes across thousands of clients.

pages.title: Distributed Consensus & Replication in SRE
bulletPoints: Strong consensus engines (Raft, Paxos, Spanner TrueTime) provide coordination for leader election and state machines.
Split-brain prevention: Strict majority quorums (N/2 + 1) guarantee that network partitions cannot elect two leaders.
Operational hazard: Taking down too many nodes for rolling upgrades can break quorum and freeze the cluster.
Monitoring consensus health: Track leader transitions, election counts, and log replication lag across regions.

pages.title: Periodic Scheduling & Distributed Cron at Scale
bulletPoints: Single-point-of-failure cron: Traditional server cron crashes if the host dies or triggers duplicate tasks upon failover.
Leader-elected distributed cron: Use Paxos/etcd to lease a single scheduler leader responsible for firing jobs.
Job idempotence: Every batch job must be idempotent or handle duplicate task deliveries without corrupting state.
Thundering herd mitigation: Avoid scheduling thousands of cron jobs at exactly 00:00:00 UTC; distribute launch minutes.

pages.title: Capacity Planning & Demand Forecasting
bulletPoints: Capacity planning ensures that sufficient hardware, network, and cloud resources exist to meet future demand.
Organic growth vs inorganic events: Track steady daily user growth vs marketing campaigns and viral spikes.
N+1 and N+2 redundancy: Ensure the service can survive the loss of one (or two) entire data centers without degradation.
Load testing: Regularly subject services to synthetic peak load benchmarks to discover hidden resource bottlenecks.

pages.title: Safe Software Deployment: Canary Releases & Rollouts
bulletPoints: Canary deployment: Direct a small fraction (e.g. 1%) of production traffic to the new binary before wide rollout.
Automated canary analysis: Compare SLIs (latency, error rates, CPU usage) between canary and baseline clusters.
Blue-Green deployments: Run two identical production environments; switch router traffic atomically once verified.
Fast rollback: The rollback mechanism must be a single-click, reliable operation that completes in under 60 seconds.

pages.title: Chaos Engineering & Fault Injection (DiRT & Chaos)
bulletPoints: Disaster Recovery Testing (DiRT): Proactively inject controlled failures into production to uncover vulnerabilities.
Netflix Chaos Monkey: Randomly terminates production instances to prove services survive spontaneous node loss.
Network chaos: Simulate packet drops, latency injection, and cross-region network partitions.
Confidence through adversity: You do not know if your failover works until you test it under real operational conditions.

pages.title: On-Call Health: Sustainable Rotations & Paging Limits
bulletPoints: Human sustainability: An SRE team should ideally have at least 8 engineers per on-call rotation to avoid burnout.
Paging budget: Aim for no more than 2 pagers per 12-hour shift on average to preserve focus and well-being.
Follow-the-Sun rotation: Distribute on-call between timezones (e.g., US and Europe/Asia) to eliminate overnight pages.
Compensation and recovery: Provide on-call pay and compensatory rest time after shifts involving overnight incidents.

pages.title: Maturing SRE: Organizational Culture & Evolution
bulletPoints: SRE is a cultural mindset of continuous improvement, rigorous measurement, and engineering-first operations.
Psychological safety: Engineers must feel safe to admit mistakes, challenge assumptions, and learn openly.
Celebrate reliability wins: Celebrate error budget surpluses and successful disaster tests alongside feature releases.
Enduring impact: Building reliable, scalable, and autonomous systems powers world-class software infrastructure.
